The Chestnut-backed antbird (Poliocrania exsul) is a medium-sized understory insectivore of humid Neotropical forests, and its life history reflects the relatively stable, low-productivity environment in which it evolved. For a passerine of its size, females attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 26.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 26.5 grams], placing it near the upper end of the mass range for typical thamnophilids. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is 3.48 grams [Ww0 = 3.48 grams], a modest initial investment that is nonetheless consistent with the relatively small clutch sizes characteristic of this lineage. Field records indicate that females lay two to five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to five eggs per clutch] but produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], an extremely low annual reproductive output compared to many temperate passerines. This constrained breeding frequency appears linked to the prolonged period of biparental care required by nestlings in the understory, as well as the relatively high rates of nest predation that favor investing in a single, well-provisioned brood.

Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration that is typical for antbirds of this body size and reflects the stable thermal conditions of the nest cavity. Upon hatching, the wet weight at birth of a nestling is about 2.6 grams [Wwb = about 2.6 grams], a value derived from the egg's dimensions—typically 22 to 24 millimeters in length and 16 to 18 millimeters in width. This altricial hatchling mass is less than ten percent of the adult female mass, highlighting the substantial growth that must occur during the nestling phase. The small initial size of the neonate is partially compensated by rapid provisioning from both parents, who deliver arthropod prey at high rates throughout the day, ensuring that the nestling accumulates mass steadily despite the challenges of a humid, pathogen-rich environment.

Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods in this species (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the developmental milestones of the nestling proceed along a well-defined schedule. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is common among antbirds, which produce altricial young that fledge before they are fully capable of independent flight, allowing them to escape the high predation pressure of the nest site. Following fledging, the young remain dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks, during which they refine their foraging skills and gradually transition to nutritional independence. The brevity of the nestling stage is a critical adaptation in a environment where nest depredation accounts for a significant proportion of reproductive failure.

Sexual maturity is attained at 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a remarkably rapid onset of gonadal development for a bird of this body size. This early puberty is likely an adaptation to the high annual mortality rates and unpredictable breeding opportunities in the understory, allowing individuals to reproduce as soon as a territory becomes available. However, the time since birth at first brood—the age at which a female successfully produces her first clutch—is considerably longer, estimated at 1.3 years [tR = 1.3 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This considerable gap between puberty and first reproduction reflects the difficulty of acquiring and defending a suitable territory in the dense, competitive understory, as well as the need to accumulate sufficient body condition to sustain the energetic demands of incubation and chick rearing.

The maximum lifespan in the wild for this species is estimated at 10.7 years [am = 10.7 years] under the same thermal regime (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a longevity that is quite typical for a Neotropical passerine of this size and life-history pace. This extended lifespan, combined with a low annual reproductive output, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survivorship rather than high fecundity. The resting metabolic rate of adult birds, measured as basal oxygen consumption at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is 52 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 52 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that falls within the expected range for a bird with an asymptotic mass of around 26.5 grams. This relatively low metabolic rate likely contributes to the species' ability to persist on a diet of arthropods in the shaded understory, where prey availability is moderate but predictable throughout the year.
